meta.description: Groucho really wrote it — this exact wording is in his 1959 memoir. But no telegram survives, and the joke was already changing shape in 1949.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I don't want to belong to any club that will accept me as a member'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, it's Groucho: the exact line appears in his own 1959 memoir. But which club, and what the original wording was, were never pinned down.

answer.sourceLine: This exact sentence is Groucho’s own: he prints it as the text of his resignation wire in his 1959 memoir Groucho and Me, at p. 321 — chapter 26, “Foot in Mouth Disease,” the chapter numbered 24 in the 1995 Da Capo reprint Quote Investigator cites. What is not settled is the event behind it — no telegram has ever surfaced, the memoir calls the club by a joke name, and the wording was already drifting when Hollywood columnists first reported the story in October 1949.

source.excerpt: PLEASE ACCEPT MY RESIGNATION. I DON’T WANT TO BELONG TO ANY CLUB THAT WILL ACCEPT ME AS A MEMBER.
trail: 20 October 1949. The joke reaches print when the Hollywood columnist Erskine Johnson reports Groucho’s resignation from the Friars’ Club as “I don’t want to belong to any club that would accept me as one of its members” — the earliest instance located by Quote Investigator ↗.

27 October 1949. One week on, Jimmie Fidler’s column in the Oregonian prints the sentence in the form Groucho himself would later print in the memoir. This and the Johnson citation were posted to the American Dialect Society list by Garson O’Toole in March 2011 ↗, alongside John Crosby’s 2 November column.

1959. Groucho tells the story himself in Groucho and Me at p. 321, chapter 26, “Foot in Mouth Disease” — the citation carried by WIST ↗. This is the first time this wording appears over Groucho’s own name.

Still missing. No telegram, wire or letter has ever been produced. Every account is a retelling — by columnists, by Groucho’s son Arthur, and by Groucho himself, who changed the club’s name when he wrote it down. QI’s verdict ↗ is that the joke is his but its original form is unrecoverable.
source.excerptNote: The telegram as Groucho prints it in Groucho and Me, in a chapter where he calls the club “the Delaney Club” — a club Quote Investigator ↗ describes as part of a humorously fictionalised account, and which WIST ↗ takes to be Groucho’s invention. Reproduced here from QI’s transcription of the passage.

author.name: Groucho Marx
author.heading: Who was Groucho Marx?
author.metaLine: 1890–1977 · American comedian, Marx Brothers star & memoirist
author.bio: Born Julius Henry Marx in New York City on 2 October 1890, Groucho went from a boy singer in vaudeville to the fast-talking, greasepaint-moustached centre of the Marx Brothers — Monkey Business, Horse Feathers, Duck Soup, A Night at the Opera. He made 26 films, 13 of them with his brothers. He then had an entire second career as a solo wit: the quiz show You Bet Your Life ran for eleven years from its 1950 television debut and was the top-rated programme by 1953. He was also a genuine writer, and Groucho and Me (1959) is his own account of the life — which is why it matters that this line appears in it.

misattribution.heading: The variants, and who added them
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of a joke pinned on the wrong man — the joke really is Groucho’s. It is a case of a joke that never had one fixed form. Here is what circulates, and where each version actually comes from.

items.who: “…any club that would have me as a member”
items.why: Probably the most-quoted form, and it is not the memoir’s. Quote Investigator ↗ traces it to Groucho’s son Arthur, who printed “Because I don’t want to belong to any club that would have me as a member!” in Collier’s in 1951 and “I just don’t want to belong to any club that would have me as a member” in Life with Groucho in 1954.

items.who: “…accept people like me as a member”
items.why: Wikiquote ↗ renders the memoir telegram with the extra words “people like me,” but QI’s transcription of the same passage ↗ does not contain them; QI records “people like me” instead in Leo Rosten’s 1950 Look profile, “I do not care to belong to a club that accepts people like me as members.”
The form given in The Groucho Letters (1967), edited by Arthur Sheekman, as recorded by Wikiquote ↗: “Please accept my resignation. I don’t care to belong to any club that will have me as a member.”

items.who: The Friars, the Lambs or Hillcrest
items.why: All three have been named, along with the “Delaney Club” of Groucho’s own telling — a club Quote Investigator ↗ describes as part of a humorously fictionalised account and WIST takes to be his invention. The earliest reports, in October 1949, say the Friars’ Club; a 1951 Los Angeles Sentinel item says the Lambs; Arthur Marx’s 1988 My Life with Groucho says Hillcrest. The Beverly Hills Tennis Club is often swept into the list, but in that same 1988 account it is the club Groucho kept — he dropped Hillcrest rather than pay dues at both.

items.who: Woody Allen — and, in the film’s own gag, Freud
items.why: Annie Hall (1977) opens with Alvy Singer calling it “the key joke of my adult life” and paraphrasing it as “I would never wanna belong to any club that would have someone like me for a member,” crediting Groucho while joking that it “appears originally in Freud’s Wit and Its Relation to the Unconscious” — see Wikiquote ↗. Many people quote the Allen paraphrase believing it is the Marx original.

Wikiquote ↗ notes the same idea in The Forsyte Saga: rejected by the ‘Hotch Potch’ for being ‘in trade,’ Old Jolyon “naturally despised the Club that did take him” — chapter II of The Man of Property ↗. That is a parallel sentiment in a novel, not a source Groucho is known to have drawn on.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is genuinely Groucho’s and this exact wording is his own, printed in Groucho and Me (1959). But no telegram or letter has ever been produced, and as Quote Investigator concludes ↗, the evidence “does not reveal the exact wording of his comical gem or the precise circumstances of its employment.”

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: The line is a resignation, not a refusal — that is the single most-lost detail. Every 1949 report describes Groucho quitting a club he already belonged to, not turning one down. Read that way the joke stops being a piece of gentle self-deprecation and becomes a small act of demolition: the moment they let him in, the place lost whatever made it worth being in.

There is a sharper reading still. Groucho was a Jewish comedian in a Hollywood where the exclusive clubs kept lists of who was acceptable, and the Hillcrest Country Club — one of the clubs later named in versions of the story — existed because the others would not have Jewish members. A joke about the worthlessness of any club that admits you lands differently when membership has been a live question your whole life.
detailsBody: The story ran through the Hollywood column circuit within a fortnight in autumn 1949 — Erskine Johnson on 20 October, Jimmie Fidler on 27 October, John Crosby on 2 November — and each columnist printed a slightly different sentence. Reader’s Digest picked up Crosby’s version in January 1950; Leo Rosten reworked it again in Look that March. The joke was mutating before anyone thought to check it.

Its second life is cinematic. Annie Hall (1977) opens with Alvy Singer calling it “the key joke of my adult life” and paraphrasing it as “I would never wanna belong to any club that would have someone like me for a member” — crediting Groucho, then adding that it may appear originally in Freud. For a very large number of people that film, not the memoir, is where they first met the line.
context.pull: The moment they let him in, the place stopped being worth belonging to.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest located instance is Erskine Johnson's Hollywood column of 20 October 1949, reporting Groucho's resignation from the Friars' Club with the wording "I don't want to belong to any club that would accept me as one of its members."

Quote Investigator reproduces the Groucho and Me (1959) passage with the telegram "PLEASE ACCEPT MY RESIGNATION. I DON'T WANT TO BELONG TO ANY CLUB THAT WILL ACCEPT ME AS A MEMBER" and states the memoir names the Delaney Club in a humorously fictionalised account.

Quote Investigator concludes that Groucho Marx crafted the line but that the evidence "does not reveal the exact wording of his comical gem or the precise circumstances of its employment," and that sources agree he was resigning rather than refusing to join.

Quote Investigator's chronology includes Jimmie Fidler (27 Oct 1949) with the exact wording "I don't want to belong to any club that will accept me as a member"; Leo Rosten in Look (28 Mar 1950) with "I do not care to belong to a club that accepts people like me as members"; Arthur Marx in Collier's (1951) and Life with Groucho (1954) with the "would have me as a member" form; and names the Friars (Oct 1949), the fictional Delaney Club (1959 memoir), the Lambs (Apr 1951, Los Angeles Sentinel) and Hillcrest (Arthur Marx, My Life with Groucho, 1988) as the clubs identified. The Beverly Hills Tennis Club appears only in that 1988 account as the second club whose dues Groucho did not want to keep paying — the club he kept, not one he resigned from.

Wikiquote cites a telegram to the Friar's Club of Beverly Hills recounted in Groucho and Me (1959), p. 321, rendering it "I DON'T WANT TO BELONG TO ANY CLUB THAT WILL ACCEPT PEOPLE LIKE ME AS A MEMBER", and gives the variant "Please accept my resignation. I don't care to belong to any club that will have me as a member" from The Groucho Letters (1967), edited by Arthur Sheekman.

Wikiquote notes an earlier parallel sentiment in John Galsworthy's The Forsyte Saga, where Old Jolyon, refused by the 'Hotch Potch' for being 'in trade', "naturally despised the Club that did take him."

Garson O'Toole's March 2011 post to the American Dialect Society list presents three 1949 antedatings: Erskine Johnson in the Dunkirk Evening Observer (20 Oct 1949), Jimmie Fidler in the Oregonian (27 Oct 1949, "I don't want to belong to any club that will accept me as a member"), and John Crosby in the St. Petersburg Times (2 Nov 1949), all reporting Groucho's resignation from the Friars' Club.

WIST cites "I don't want to belong to any club that will accept me as a member" to Groucho and Me, chapter 26, "Foot in Mouth Disease" (1959), and notes that Groucho's book called the club the Delaney Club while others named the Friars Club or Hillcrest Country Club.

Project Gutenberg's text of The Man of Property, chapter II "Old Jolyon Goes to the Opera", contains: "He had always had a contempt for the place, having joined it many years ago when they refused to have him at the 'Hotch Potch' owing to his being 'in trade.' ... He naturally despised the Club that did take him."

The Internet Archive catalogue record for Groucho and Me lists the author as Marx, Groucho, 1890-1977; publication date 1959; publisher B. Geis Associates, distributed by Random House, New York; 344 pages; access-restricted.

Wikipedia states Groucho Marx was born Julius Henry Marx on 2 October 1890 in New York City and died 19 August 1977; he made 26 films, 13 with his brothers, including Monkey Business, Horse Feathers, Duck Soup and A Night at the Opera; You Bet Your Life moved to television on 5 October 1950 and ran eleven years, topping the ratings by 1953; and he published the autobiography Groucho and Me in 1959.

Wikiquote's Annie Hall page records Alvy Singer crediting Groucho Marx for "the key joke of my adult life," paraphrasing it as "I would never wanna belong to any club that would have someone like me for a member," and saying it appears originally in Freud's Wit and Its Relation to the Unconscious.
AbeBooks dealer listing gives the first edition bibliographic details as Groucho and Me by Groucho Marx (Julius Henry Marx), Bernard Geis Associates, New York, 1959, first edition, 344 pp.
